design: 7 published doctoral dissertation excerpts; norm or concept research objects; no whole theses stored
verification: Quoted short phrases cross-read against university-hosted PDF text via public web viewing; NOT reverified by the Python runtime from original PDF bytes

cases.author: T. Liau
cases.author_note: Oxford repository identifies author as T. Liau. Do not infer unverified given names.
cases.title: Standing in Private Law
cases.object_title: Standing as a power distinct from a claim-right
cases.locus: Ch 1 pp 5–7; Ch 2 concepts; discussion of exceptions in tort chapter
reconstructed: The author's standing/right distinction explains standing as an enforcement power rather than a claim-right.
The thesis argues that a general standing rule is implicit within private-law doctrine.
In the ordinary case it is the primary right-holder who can enforce the underlying right, while the thesis accommodates exceptional circumstances.
cases.warrant: The distinction between rights and litigation powers, if doctrinally supported, helps explain who may enforce rights; exceptions require careful qualification.
cases.challenge: The conceptual separability of standing and a right does not alone prove an exclusive right-holder rule in each doctrinal area.
cases.reply: The thesis expressly offers private-law doctrinal examinations and allows exceptions; this is a request to inspect those analyses, not evidence that they are absent.
cases.depth: selected original PDF passages, multiple chapters

cases.author: Laura J Downey
cases.title: Emerging Legal Concepts at the Nexus of Law, Technology and Society: A Case Study in Identity
cases.object_title: Identity as potentially emerging legal concept
cases.jurisdiction: UK with Scottish law and biomedical technologies
cases.locus: Abstract; Ch 5 emerging legal concepts, near PDF p124; Ch 6 identity
reconstructed: Identity is used across several overlapping senses and is context dependent.
Even absent unequivocal formal UK legal recognition, observable discourse and institutional contexts may indicate an emerging legal concept.
The thesis tracks possible concept emergence and expressly distinguishes its project from advocating identity as a mandatory rule for future regulation.
cases.warrant: An identified concept can be studied for emerging recognition through sufficiently specified indicators without requiring a proposed new duty.
cases.challenge: When does recurrent social and policy discourse count as emerging legal conceptual recognition rather than merely an external vocabulary?
cases.reply: The work develops an explicit emergence-factor framework and considers authority, legality and legitimacy; those passages must be examined before declaring a gap.
cases.depth: abstract and selected Ch 5/6 PDF passages

cases.author: Catriona A. W. McMillan
cases.title: The Human Embryo in Vitro: A Processual Entity in Legal Stasis
cases.object_title: Legal status of in vitro embryo and regulatory stasis
cases.temporal_scope: Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 (as amended), as discussed in 2018 thesis
cases.locus: Abstract; Ch 4 printed pp148–149; further interpretive caveats around printed p173–174
reconstructed: The author diagnoses a conceptual gap between a regulated embryo's processual situation and the framework's underlying legal categorisation.
The argument challenges treating different embryo processes under a single legal special-status construction.
The project proposes examining alternative conceptual approaches while qualifying the discussion as possibilities, not a mandatory prescribed reform.
cases.warrant: A diagnosed mismatch may justify further conceptual inquiry, but does not by itself make one statutory reform obligatory.
cases.challenge: Does the regulator need an ontologically complete embryo classification, or can legally stipulated boundaries remain justified despite biological variation?
cases.reply: The author distinguishes partial conceptual reframing from reproducing every biological change and states that some final implications are possible rather than mandatory.
cases.depth: abstract and selected original PDF passages from Ch 4 and later discussion

cases.author: Sjur Kristoffer Dyrkolbotn
cases.title: On the Legitimacy of Economic Development Takings
cases.object_title: Public-interest conditions and procedural legitimacy in expropriation
cases.jurisdiction: England and Wales; US; ECtHR and Norway (comparative study)
cases.temporal_scope: legal systems as examined in thesis dated 2016
cases.locus: Ch 1 section 1.5 printed pp29–30; abstract; Part I judicial review
anchors: public use, public interest and public purpose
reconstructed: Terms public use, public interest and public purpose may carry jurisdiction-dependent content and must not be collapsed uncritically.
The dissertation contends that a legitimacy criterion for economic takings includes inclusive decision-making as well as public benefit.
Participation of owners and affected dependants is offered as a normative criterion for legitimate takings, not simply a universal test of formal validity.
cases.warrant: A participation-based account of legitimacy can build on a normative premise of equitable decision-making while keeping each jurisdiction's validity test distinct.
cases.challenge: Does a normative requirement of participatory fairness follow as a binding positive-law condition in every studied jurisdiction, or only as the author's justification criterion?
cases.reply: The thesis explicitly distinguishes jurisdictional terms and frames participation as an argued legitimacy standard, not a blanket claim of invalidity in every state.
cases.depth: original PDF abstract and Ch 1 printed pp29–30

cases.author: David Frydrych
cases.title: The Architecture of Rights
cases.object_title: Relationship between legal rights, powers and enforceability
cases.jurisdiction: analytical legal jurisprudence, with reference to legal rights
cases.locus: Abstract printed p ii; Ch 6–8 on legal-right enforceability and liberties
anchors: not invariably enforceable by legal powers
reconstructed: The author distinguishes existence of a legal right from the availability of legal powers as means of enforcing it.
Wholly unenforceable legal rights are analysed as defective or imperfect cases rather than automatically non-rights.
The dissertation considers liberty-based claiming and invocation as ways legal rights may have practical significance apart from legal powers.
cases.warrant: The account requires independent criteria for what makes an instance of right genuine, imperfect or defective, not a stipulative label alone.
cases.challenge: If enforceability is not necessary, what conceptual criteria prevent any moral interest or unenforceable aspiration being counted as a legal right?
cases.reply: The author expressly discusses the imperfect-right boundary and alternative forms of claiming, so a reviewer must engage Chapters 6–8 before alleging arbitrariness.
cases.depth: original PDF abstract and targeted conceptual chapters

cases.author: Carmine Conte
cases.title: Penalties Reworked: The Rule Against Penalties Restated, Justified and Refined
cases.object_title: The penalty rule governing agreed damages clauses
cases.jurisdiction: English and Australian private contract law
cases.temporal_scope: doctrine examined as of 2014; later UKSC 2015 decision requires separate current-law check
cases.locus: Abstract printed p ii, Ch 1 pp3–7; Ch 11 discussion of partial unenforceability
reconstructed: The thesis distinguishes valid liquidated-damages clauses from clauses falling under the penalty doctrine.
The author's refined interpretive account emphasizes detriment manifestly excessive relative to the legitimate function of a clause.
The thesis argues the effect of a penal clause is partial unenforceability rather than a simple undifferentiated nullity.
cases.warrant: Case-law fit, structure and contractual remediation must justify the refinement; the law-in-force date is indispensable to its doctrinal status.
cases.challenge: What does the later UK Supreme Court ruling Cavendish/ParkingEye [2015] UKSC 67 change in the test, remedy and scope? The 2014 thesis cannot be condemned for not citing a 2015 judgment.
cases.reply: The dissertation confines its investigation to the law then available and provides extensive interpretive case-law analysis; updates must be temporally labelled.
cases.depth: original PDF abstract and selected chapter discussions; primary 2015 UKSC comparator

cases.author: Gehan Gunatilleke
cases.title: Justifying Limitations on the Freedom to Manifest Religion or Belief and the Freedom of Expression under the ICCPR
cases.jurisdiction: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
cases.temporal_scope: treaty interpretation and Human Rights Committee practice examined circa 2020
cases.locus: Abstract printed p ii; Ch 2 around pp77–80 (duty-based argument)
reconstructed: The ICCPR authorizes restrictions on the two freedoms only on the legal grounds and conditions stated in its limitation clauses.
The author gives a normative reason for requiring public justification of competing interests before coercing an individual.
The author proposes that restriction decisions establish sufficient reason for the individual to bear a duty of justice to refrain from the conduct.
cases.warrant: A duty-based criterion is argued through public reasons and the structure of rights and correlative duties, but its fit with treaty text and Human Rights Committee practice remains separately disputable.
cases.challenge: Does a duty-of-justice standard interpret ICCPR limitation clauses faithfully, or add a contested justificatory burden that treaty text does not legally require?
cases.reply: The author examines drafting, accepted interpretations and Human Rights Committee decisions, and expressly proposes a good-faith interpretive argument; no missing-normative-bridge conclusion may be assumed.
cases.depth: original PDF abstract and selected Chapter 2 discussion
